present: A normal declarative main clause has one first constituent and then its finite verb. The subject can be that first constituent. Other phrases can appear inside the verb bracket.
English often uses a similar subject–verb order, but Dutch keeps the finite verb second when another complete phrase comes first.
fronted: The complete time, place or object phrase is one first constituent. The finite verb follows it, then the subject: second position means a constituent, not the second written word.
English can keep subject before verb after an initial time phrase; Dutch uses inversion here.
question: Question word and inversion
A question word/phrase comes first, then the finite verb and subject. In a subject question the question phrase itself is the subject, so no extra subject is needed.
English often inserts do/does; Dutch normally puts the finite verb before the subject instead.
yes-no: The finite verb starts a neutral yes/no question, followed by the subject. When subject je/jij follows a present verb, the ordinary added second-person -t is omitted; a t belonging to the stem stays (laat je). Formal u does not follow that inversion rule.
Dutch inverts the existing finite verb rather than adding English do/does.
modal: The modal is finite and occupies the main-clause verb position. The other action is an infinitive without te, normally toward the end of its clause.
English can/must/may also take a bare infinitive, but Dutch can place the object and time phrases before that final infinitive.
modal-question: The finite modal comes before the subject. The requested action stays an infinitive without te. Whether this asks about ability, permission or willingness depends on the actual modal and context.
English can/could/may are not interchangeable in every situation; preserve the intended ability or permission distinction.
polite: Zou/zouden introduces a tentative or polite question; the subject follows the finite verb. Kunnen and the requested action can form a final bare-infinitive cluster. A request does not assert that the action is completed.
English could/would soften a request too; Dutch zou/zouden is not a simple claim that the action happened in the past.
perfect: The finite auxiliary is in the main-clause verb position. Its object, pronouns and other phrases can stand before the participle that closes the bracket. Auxiliary choice depends on the actual verb and meaning.
English past reporting may correspond to Dutch perfect; Dutch often puts the object before the final participle.
past: The finite past form occupies the ordinary main-clause verb position. Its number agrees with the subject. The past event belongs to the context supplied, not automatically to every repeated or present situation.
Dutch uses a single finite past verb here; English did is not added to the Dutch construction.
past-question: The finite past verb and subject invert in this question. A question phrase, when present, precedes the finite verb. Keep the particular past event distinct from a present repeated problem.
English may use did plus an infinitive; Dutch uses its finite past form.
future: The finite future/intention verb occupies the main-clause verb position; the intended action is a bare infinitive. A future commitment is not a report of completed work.
English will or be going to expresses a future intention; Dutch can also use the present with an explicit future time.
subordinate: The main clause retains its own finite-verb position. The conjunction introduces a separate clause whose subject and other material precede its finite verb or verb group. The conjunction's meaning must fit the situation.
English usually keeps subject–verb–object inside the embedded clause; Dutch moves the finite verb/group toward its end.
subordinate-first: The complete subordinate clause counts as the first constituent of the main clause. The main finite verb follows it, then the main subject. Inside the subordinate clause its own verb/group comes toward the end.
English can keep the main subject before the verb after an initial when/if/because clause; Dutch uses main-clause inversion.
imperative: A normal spoken imperative starts with the verb stem and usually leaves the addressed subject unspoken. Objects and other phrases follow; a separable particle goes later in the main clause.
English also commonly gives instructions without an explicit you. Polite wording and the situation determine the register.
separable: The finite verb stands in the main-clause verb position while its separable particle appears later. The infinitive and participle join the particle to the verb; te goes between particle and infinitive.
English phrasal verbs sometimes split too, but Dutch separability belongs to the particular verb, not to every prefix.
progressive: A finite form of zijn describes the ongoing state. Aan het is followed by an infinitive, not an extra finite verb. For separable verbs more than one progressive placement can be natural.
English be plus an -ing form often corresponds to Dutch zijn aan het plus infinitive.
bezig: A finite form of zijn plus bezig describes an ongoing activity. Met takes an activity noun/nominalised infinitive; a te-infinitive construction names the action directly. Do not confuse met with the conjunction terwijl.
English busy working or working on can correspond to bezig met or bezig te; choose the construction actually written here.
om-te: Om introduces an infinitive phrase with te. Its object can come before the infinitive; with a separable verb te stands between its particle and verb. This is not a second finite clause.
English often uses to plus a verb for purpose where Dutch uses om ... te.
te: A verb or adjective can take a complement containing te plus an infinitive; an adjective itself is never a finite verb. A separable infinitive places te between its particle and verb. Contrast modals, which normally take a bare infinitive.
English and Dutch do not require to/te after exactly the same verbs; learn the particular combination.
reflexive: The reflexive pronoun belongs to the verb's subject: ik–me, je–je, hij/zij–zich, we–ons. A separable reflexive verb still splits in a main clause.
An English expression may omit a reflexive where Dutch requires one, such as zich afvragen or zich voelen.
er: Er can introduce the existence/appearance of something, or combine with a preposition to refer back to a thing. These are different functions; agreement and meaning depend on the actual sentence.
English there can introduce existence, while English about it/on it may correspond to a Dutch er-plus-preposition combination.
negation: Geen negates an indefinite noun phrase or an uncountable amount. Niet negates a verb/state or another specific constituent. Nog niet means not yet; niet meer means no longer. The position depends on the intended scope.
English often uses not or no where Dutch distinguishes niet from geen.
possession: A possessive refers to the owner, while ons/onze follows the noun: ons for a singular het-word, onze for de-words and plurals. Adjective endings depend on the article, definiteness and noun gender.
English our does not vary with noun gender; Dutch ons/onze does.
comparison: The comparison/quantity phrase names the relevant degree or amount. A Dutch comparative commonly uses dan for the comparison, while the positive equality pattern uses even ... als.
English than corresponds to dan in a standard comparative; as ... as corresponds to even ... als.
proposal: Laten we invites the speaker and others to act together. The requested action is a bare infinitive; the proposal does not report that the action has already been completed.
English let's plus infinitive corresponds naturally to Dutch laten we plus infinitive.
passive: A finite passive auxiliary plus a participle focuses on what receives the action. Wordt/worden describes an action in the present; is/zijn plus a participle can describe a completed result depending on context.
English be plus participle and Dutch worden/zijn plus participle need a context-sensitive tense interpretation.
past-perfect: Had/hadden plus a participle reports an event completed before another past reference point. A following toen/nadat clause helps place those events in order.
English had plus participle has the corresponding earlier-past meaning; do not substitute a present perfect without changing that reference point.
